reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it presents and demonstrates a purported Wish method for obtaining sneakers, electronics, and other goods for free, tied to following the process and potentially paying shipping. It also discusses free-shipping codes and urges viewers to act before the method is fixed. Although the speaker says he does not promote the scam, the same segment presents the method directly to viewers.

citations.quote: we just hacked the system again!
I'm just gonna show you guys how to get stuff for free
there's a bunch of shit that is just a hundred percent free that only thing is you need to pay shipping
here's where the scam comes into play which I do not promote
we're just gonna add it to the cart

opening.argument: The speaker expressly distances himself from deceptive conduct rather than presenting it as an endorsed fraud: he says the alleged scam is something he “do[es] not promote,” and separately retracts the dangerous relationship joke by saying “Don’t do that actually it’s a bad joke.” The video also contains uncertainty about the shipping-code process, including that the speaker’s attempted code “doesn’t work anymore.” That combination supports an investigative or cautionary presentation of a claimed loophole, not a reliable promise that viewers will receive goods without cost or risk.

citations.quote: here's where the scam comes into play which I do not promote
Don't do that actually it's a bad joke
mine i just tried today and it doesn't work anymore

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution treats colorful language as proof of endorsement, but “hacked the system” is rhetoric, not proof that a fraudulent method worked. Likewise, saying the video will show viewers how to get items for free describes the subject under examination; it does not establish a guaranteed result. The speaker’s express statement that he does not promote the scam is directly relevant context, while adding an item to a cart only shows an attempted transaction.

citations.quote: we just hacked the system again!
I'm just gonna show you guys how to get stuff for free
here's where the scam comes into play which I do not promote
we're just gonna add it to the cart

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The disclaimer is overwhelmed by the conduct and framing that surround it. The speaker calls the activity a system hack, promises to show viewers how to obtain goods for free, and immediately proceeds to add an item to the cart. Saying “I do not promote” the scam does not negate directly presenting the claimed method or urging viewers to pursue it.

citations.quote: we just hacked the system again!
I'm just gonna show you guys how to get stuff for free
here's where the scam comes into play which I do not promote
we're just gonna add it to the cart

opening.argument: The material is structured as a demonstration of an online shopping process: the speaker says he will show how the result is obtained, then moves through Wish search results, product pages, and a cart, followed by an unboxing. The frames likewise show a Wish search for “free sneaker,” a shopping cart, and physical items being displayed. That is consistent with testing and documenting a purported website behavior. The evidence does not establish that every advertised item arrived, that the method was repeatable, or that viewers were promised a guaranteed outcome.

citations.quote: I'm just gonna show you guys how to get stuff for free
I got like 30 things for free off of this website
only going to unbox a few things at the end of this video

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution’s selected quotations identify the topic and the act of adding a product, but they do not distinguish a demonstration from an inducement. The visible search and cart screens document what was tried, not whether the claimed bypass was valid or whether viewers would succeed. The speaker also says only a few items will be unboxed, leaving the broader claim unverified.

citations.quote: only going to unbox a few things at the end of this video
we're just gonna add it to the cart
a lot of it hasn't come in yet

true_side_reply.rebuttal: This is not merely neutral testing. The speaker explicitly says he will show viewers how to get things for free, describes the process as a “little heist,” and tells viewers to act quickly before the method is fixed. A partial unboxing does not weaken the instructional message; it supplies apparent proof while the central acquisition claim is being promoted.

citations.quote: I'm just gonna show you guys how to get stuff for free
perform a little heist
i want to do this before they fix this

opening.argument: The concrete activity shown is ordinary retail browsing and purchasing on Wish, with listed products, quantities, sizes, shipping, and a cart. The speaker specifically says the items are not simply costless because “you need to pay shipping,” and the frames show products in a normal shopping interface and a cart. The record does not show a deposit, credential request, downline, guaranteed return, or other classic financial extraction mechanism. At most, it presents a disputed discount or pricing loophole involving merchandise and shipping.

citations.quote: there's a bunch of shit that is just a hundred percent free that only thing is you need to pay shipping
we're just gonna add it to the cart

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the products ordinary merchandise does not resolve the central claim. The video’s unusual proposition is not that Wish sells products, but that a supposed loophole makes them free. Shipping and promo codes are part of that claimed acquisition method, and the speaker encourages resale of the items. The absence of a deposit or downline is therefore beside the point.

citations.quote: how I found it. I searched free
you bring it to Play-doh's closet and you saw it's them and you get money for this free stuff
promo codes that give you free shipping

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The relevant mechanism is still a purported low-cost acquisition scheme, even without a deposit or pyramid structure. The speaker says products are “a hundred percent free,” describes obtaining many items, discusses resale for cash, and seeks a free-shipping code. The ordinary shopping interface is the vehicle for the claim, not evidence that the claim is ordinary commerce.
